pageData.title: The Kingdom of Tonga
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Tonga. The Kingdom of Tonga was forged by Taufa'ahau, a chief converted to Christianity in 1831 by Methodist missionaries, who became Tu'i Kanokupolu and took the title King George Tupou I. During his long reign Tonga became a unified and independent country with a modern constitution in 1875, a legal code, and an administrative structure, and a series of treaties - including one with the United States in 1888 - recognized Tonga's sovereignty. The kingdom matters because it achieved what almost no other Pacific state did: it modernized entirely on its own terms as a sovereign state, and its monarchy is unique in the Pacific Islands for having been a constitutional monarchy since 1875. The missionaries had not found it easy - the London Missionary Society and a Methodist mission failed in 1797 and 1822 before a renewed Methodist effort succeeded in 1826 - but Christianity became central to Tongan national identity.
pageData.para2: In 1900, during the reign of George II, Tonga became a British protectorate to discourage German advances, though it kept its own monarchy and was never formally colonized. George II was followed in 1918 by Queen Salote Tupou III, who ruled until her death in 1965, admired by the Tongan people and charming the British at Queen Elizabeth II's coronation. Tonga regained its full independence in 1970, remaining a sovereign Polynesian monarchy within the Commonwealth. Its royal traditions, its church, and cultural treasures like the lakalaka - the sung speeches and dances inscribed by UNESCO as a masterpiece of intangible heritage - remain at the heart of national life in one of the very few Pacific states never fully colonized by any power.

pageData.title: French Polynesia
pageData.para1: French Polynesia. French Polynesia is the French overseas collectivity of the South Pacific, a scattering of archipelagos - the Society Islands, the Tuamotus, the Marquesas, the Gambiers, and the Austral Islands - around the great island of Tahiti, seat of the Pomare dynasty. France moved in through the missionary question: after French Catholic missionaries landed in 1834 and were expelled in 1836, France sent a gunboat in 1838, and in 1842 Tahiti and Tahuata were declared a French protectorate; the capital of Papeete was founded in 1843. In 1880 France annexed Tahiti outright, changing its status from protectorate to colony, and the remaining archipelagos followed - the Leeward Islands in 1888, and the last holdouts, which had lobbied unsuccessfully for British protection, in 1889. Its archipelagos span immense distances: the Marquesas lie 1,450 kilometers northeast of Tahiti, and the Tuamotus alone comprise some 80 low coral atolls, of which only Rangiroa, with its airport, is in close contact with the capital.
pageData.para2: The colony became the Territory of French Polynesia in 1957. In 1962, when Algerian independence made France's early nuclear testing ground unusable, Moruroa atoll in the Tuamotus was selected as the new testing site, and nuclear tests - conducted underground after 1974 - scarred the territory's politics and environment for decades. Autonomy grew in stages: an internal autonomy statute in 1977, and in 2004 an administrative autonomy that made it an 'overseas country' of the French Republic. Independence movements exist but have not succeeded, and the economy rests on tourism, on the lagoons' fish and mother-of-pearl, and above all on the cultivation of black pearls in the Tuamotu and Gambier Islands, which accounts for a large portion of export earnings. The territory is France's sole 'overseas country' - though the United Nations classifies it as a non-self-governing territory.

pageData.title: German New Guinea
pageData.para1: German New Guinea. German New Guinea was Germany's Pacific colony in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, covering the northeastern quadrant of New Guinea with the Bismarck Archipelago and the northern Solomons. By 1884 the German New Guinea Company was administering the northeastern quadrant - in the same year Britain declared a protectorate over the southeastern quadrant, later administered by Australia from 1906 - and it was in the island territories, especially after the imperial government took over in 1899, that most early economic activity took place: plantations were widely established in the New Guinea islands and around Madang, worked by laborers drawn from across the region. The chartered company's rule drew criticism for doing little to encourage colonial investment. The colony matters as the Pacific's brief but consequential German moment, ended by the First World War after barely thirty years.
pageData.para2: Australian forces seized the colony in 1914, and in 1921 Australian control of the northeastern quadrant was formalized as a League of Nations mandate, administered separately from Papua to the south. The discovery in the 1920s of massive gold deposits at the Bulolo River brought a rush of activity that hit the mandated territory far harder than Papua, and the Highlanders were utilized as a massive new source of labour for the coastal plantations. The Japanese invaded northern New Guinea in early 1942 and took the territorial headquarters at Rabaul before being defeated by the Allies, primarily Australian troops. After the war the territories were gradually brought together - with new crops like Arabica coffee spreading among local smallholders from the 1950s - until they merged into the independent state of Papua New Guinea.

pageData.title: European Exploration of the Pacific
pageData.para1: European Exploration of the Pacific. European exploration of the Pacific was the centuries-long sequence of maritime expeditions - Spanish, Dutch, French, and British - that opened the world's largest ocean to European maps from the 16th to the 18th century. It began with Ferdinand Magellan, whose Spanish expedition of 1519-22 achieved the first circumnavigation of the globe, though Magellan himself was killed in what is today the Philippines and only 22 of the original crew sailed the whole way home. Behind the voyages lay the search for the Terra Australis Incognita, the theoretical Southern Continent that appeared on world maps as early as 1508 - for without such a counterweight, many believed, the world would simply tip up. The Dutch exploration culminated in Abel Tasman's voyage of 1642-43, which sailed south of the Australian continent and encountered Tasmania and New Zealand.
pageData.para2: The eighteenth century brought systematic science: French expeditions under Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1766-69), Jean-Francois de La Perouse (1785-88), and d'Entrecasteaux (1791-93), British voyages under Samuel Wallis and Philip Carteret (1767-68), and above all the Englishman James Cook, by far the most wide-ranging of them all, who made three separate voyages to the Pacific in 1768-71, 1772-75, and 1776-80. One of Cook's most important achievements was finally to prove that the Southern Continent did not exist; the Hawaiian Islands, missed by all earlier routes, were not seen by Europeans until his last voyage. These expeditions carried scientists and artists who cataloged new lands, peoples, and natural history, while scurvy and rudimentary navigation made every voyage a gamble with death - and their maps and reports set the direct stage for the missionary activity, colonial annexation, and political transformation of Oceania that followed.

pageData.title: Colonial Australia & Penal Settlements
pageData.para1: Colonial Australia & Penal Settlements. Colonial Australia began as a solution to a British problem: having transported about 50,000 convicts to the New World between 1718 and 1775, Britain lost that outlet with American independence and searched for an alternative. In August 1786 the Pitt government announced its intention to send convicts to Botany Bay - a site recommended by Joseph Banks, who had accompanied Cook on his 1770 voyage - and on January 26, 1788, the First Fleet under Captain Arthur Phillip founded the penal settlement at Sydney Cove. Over eighty years, between 1787 and 1868, around 166,000 men, women, and children were sent to the convict colonies; the system applied even to children from the age of nine, and its stated logic was rehabilitation through forced labour - convicts built the colony's farms, wharves, and roads.
pageData.para2: By 1820 British settlement was still largely confined to a 100-kilometer arc around Sydney and the central plain of Van Diemen's Land, but from 1816 penal transportation increased rapidly and the number of free settlers grew steadily - by 1850 the settler population of New South Wales had grown to 180,000. New colonies followed at Western Australia in 1829 and South Australia and the Port Phillip District in 1836. Transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840 amid public demands for representative government, and a semi-elected Legislative Council was established. The expansion of cattle and sheep grazing inland came at devastating cost to Indigenous Australians through introduced diseases, violent conflict, and the dispossession of their traditional lands - a dispossession met by sustained Aboriginal resistance. Gold rushes in the 1850s then transformed the colonies' economies and accelerated democratic reform, and in 1901 the six self-governing colonies federated to form the Commonwealth of Australia.

pageData.title: The Treaty of Waitangi & the New Zealand Wars
pageData.para1: The Treaty of Waitangi & the New Zealand Wars. The Treaty of Waitangi, considered the founding document of New Zealand, was signed in the Bay of Islands on February 6, 1840, by Captain William Hobson, several English residents, and some forty-five Maori rangatira - the first of about 540 chiefs to sign - after ground prepared since 1833 by James Busby, the first British official on the islands, who forged alliances with local chiefs. Its three articles provided for the Maori signatories' acceptance of the British queen's sovereignty, the Crown's protection of Maori possessions with the exclusive right to buy their land, and the promise of the same rights as all British subjects. The treaty matters deeply because it remains the foundational - and continuously contested - constitutional document of modern New Zealand.
pageData.para2: In May 1840 Hobson proclaimed British sovereignty over New Zealand, and everything changed: the influx of settlers was so great that land became scarce, and the government bought Maori land at meager prices to sell to settlers at a profit. In 1844 the Northern War broke out when the Ngapuhi chief Hone Heke Pokai - the treaty's first signatory - and his men chopped down the British flagstaff; wider wars followed across the islands until 1872. The British proceeded to confiscate almost half a million hectares of Maori land, some even belonging to tribes that had not fought, devastating Maori economic power for generations - the novelist Anthony Trollope, traveling through New Zealand in 1872 at the end of the war, described what he saw as a people robbed of their future. Twentieth-century treaty settlements would begin the long process of redress.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Hawaii & Annexation
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Hawaii & Annexation. The Kingdom of Hawaii was the sovereign nation established when Kamehameha the Great united the islands in 1795, ending years of interisland conflict, and completed in 1810 with the peaceful absorption of Kauai. Through the nineteenth century the unified kingdom navigated the pressures of the imperial Pacific - while American investors came to own many of the islands' sugarcane fields and successfully lobbied Washington in their interest; Hawaiian sugar exports soared from some 20 million pounds in the 1870s to over 200 million by 1890, and the United States extracted a naval base at Pearl Harbor, which the king accepted under duress. When domestic sugar-beet producers convinced Congress to favor them, Hawaiian sugar was left at a competitive disadvantage, and Native Hawaiians had become a minority in their own islands by the 1890s as Asian laborers migrated to work the fields.
pageData.para2: In 1893 Queen Lili'uokalani introduced a new constitution expanding the rights of native Hawaiians, and the sugar planters used her reforms as a pretext to seize power: US Marines armed with Gatling guns surrounded the queen's palace, and hoping to prevent bloodshed she yielded, while the pineapple magnate Sanford Dole agreed to lead the new government. The takeover divided America - the Senate, disturbed by how power had been seized, delayed the annexation treaty to hear the queen's representative, and President Cleveland opposed what Harrison had favored - but McKinley won the 1896 election as an annexationist, and when war with Spain broke out in 1898 the political climate changed entirely: annexation was resubmitted as a resolution requiring only a simple majority, and passed. Hawaii became a US territory, and in 1959 the 50th state.
